nameStory: The lined orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive striped patterns that run across its body and legs, creating clear lines that help distinguish it from other orbweavers. These markings look almost like someone drew parallel lines with a fine-tipped pen across the spider's surface.
description: The lined orbweaver is a small, compact spider that builds classic circular orb webs between plants and shrubs. Its body features prominent dark and light striped patterns that make it quite recognizable among New England's orbweavers. This diminutive spider typically measures less than half an inch in body length, making it one of the smaller members of the orbweaver family you'll encounter in our region.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for distinct dark and light stripes running across the abdomen and legs, creating a lined appearance that feels almost geometric when you observe it closely

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds small but perfectly circular orb webs, typically 4-6 inches across, with sticky capture spirals that feel tacky to the touch if accidentally encountered

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and compact spider with a body rarely exceeding 6mm, roughly the size of a small peppercorn

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, somewhat flattened abdomen that appears almost button-like when viewed from above, with relatively short, sturdy legs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits at the center of its web during daylight hours, unlike many orbweavers that hide at the web's edge

habitat: Found in gardens, woodland edges, and areas with mixed vegetation where they can string their webs between shrubs, tall grasses, and herbaceous plants. They prefer somewhat protected spots with moderate moisture, often building webs 1-3 feet off the ground in areas that receive partial sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, with females starting to build their characteristic small orb webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mature spiders are most visible in their webs, actively hunting and mating throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs before the first hard frosts, while adults gradually become less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs or spiderlings in protected locations under leaf litter or bark.

funFact: Despite being frequently mistaken for the much more common Cyclosa turbinata, lined orbweavers can actually be distinguished by gently breathing on their web - the perfectly symmetrical construction and smaller size becomes immediately apparent when the web moves, unlike the more irregular repairs typical of Cyclosa webs.
confusionNotes: Commonly misidentified as Cyclosa turbinata due to similar size and orb web construction. The key difference is in the body markings - lined orbweavers have distinct parallel stripes while Cyclosa has more mottled, irregular patterns. Memory trick: 'Lines are fine, mottled is Cyclosa.'
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the identification challenges that make spider watching rewarding - what appears to be a 'common' orbweaver at first glance often turns out to be something much less frequently noticed when you look closely at the details.
compareHints: Among its Mangora relatives, the lined orbweaver's striped pattern is more pronounced than the tuft-legged orbweaver's subtle markings, and lacks the distinctive green coloration of the green-legged orbweaver. Its geometric stripe pattern is the most regular and defined of any New England Mangora species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Mangora relatives, the Tuft-legged Orbweaver is distinguished by having the most prominent leg tufts and more subdued coloring.
